title: NY State Senate · District 28
area: Manhattan's East Side, including the Upper East Side, Yorkville, Midtown East, Murray Hill, Kips Bay, and Gramercy.

context.text: Incumbent Liz Krueger (D) advanced without a primary opponent; Alina Bonsell (R, Block Mamdani Party) also advanced without a primary opponent. Krueger is not running on the Working Families Party line this cycle.

candidates.name: Liz Krueger
candidates.currentRole: New York State Senator, District 28 (since 2013); previously District 26 (2002-2013)

summary.text: Liz Krueger is the Democratic incumbent seeking re-election to NY Senate District 28. A former anti-hunger advocate who directed the New York City Food Bank, she first won her seat in a 2002 special election after narrowly losing in 2000, and has chaired the Senate Finance Committee since the Democrats took the majority in 2018-2019. She has focused on tax and budget policy, affordable housing, reproductive health, climate legislation, and hunger/anti-poverty programs.

background.text: Born November 20, 1957, in Ridgewood, New Jersey; graduated from Ridgewood High School in 1975.

Earned a B.S. in social policy/human development from Northwestern University (1979) and a master's degree in public policy from the University of Chicago (1981); her official Senate biography identifies the graduate school as the University of Chicago's Harris Graduate School of Public Policy.

Before holding office, worked on hunger and anti-poverty issues: researcher for the Children's Policy Research Project at the University of Chicago (1980-1981), Special Project Coordinator for the Greater Cleveland Community Food Bank (1981-1983), consultant to the board of Food for Survival, and Associate Director of the Community Food Resource Center (1986-2000).

Was the founding director of the New York City Food Bank, and chaired the New York City Food Stamp Task Force and co-facilitated the New York City Welfare Reform Network, according to her official Senate biography.
First ran for the State Senate in 2000, narrowly losing to incumbent Republican Roy Goodman; won the seat in a 2002 special election after Goodman resigned.
Represented District 26 from her 2002 election until redistricting, and has represented District 28 since 2013.
Elected Chair of the Senate Finance Committee after Democrats won the Senate majority in 2018; in 2025-2026 she also sits on the Budget and Revenue and Rules committees.
Her official biography lists her as founding co-chair of the New York State Bipartisan Pro-Choice Legislative Caucus and as a 2026 honoree of the New York State Senate Veterans' Hall of Fame.
According to her official biography, she lives on Manhattan's East Side with her husband, John E. Seley, a retired professor of urban planning and geography at the CUNY Graduate Center.

priorities.text: Tax and government reform: modernizing New York State's governmental processes, electoral system, and tax policy.
Healthcare and reproductive rights, including leadership on the Reproductive Health Act and postpartum depression legislation.
Protecting and expanding affordable housing and addressing homelessness.
Climate and environmental policy, including the Climate Change Superfund Act, a fracking ban, a plastic bag ban, and fossil-fuel divestment from state pension funds.
Hunger and anti-poverty policy, including expanding SNAP access and opposing federal cuts to food assistance.

positions.summary: Sponsored the Climate Change Superfund Act and a statewide fracking ban, pushed fossil-fuel divestment from state pensions, sponsored the Solar UP Now NY Act to expand portable solar devices, and opposes shifting the cost of new nuclear power plants onto ratepayers and taxpayers.
Cited as a leader on New York's Reproductive Health Act and related reproductive-health legislation.
Stated priority of protecting and expanding affordable housing for New Yorkers and addressing homelessness.
Advocates for improved healthcare access as part of her legislative priorities.

record.text: Chairs the Senate Finance Committee, a post she has held since 2019; also serves on the Budget and Revenue and Rules committees in the 2025-2026 session.

Sponsored S8512C, the Solar UP Now NY Act, creating a regulatory framework for portable solar generation devices and exempting them from interconnection/net-metering requirements; passed the Senate 62-0 on April 21, 2026 and was substituted by Assembly companion A9111C, which passed the Assembly 59-1 on May 28, 2026.
Joined 69 state lawmakers in a September 2026 letter urging New York's congressional delegation to reverse federal SNAP cuts.
Publicly opposed proposals to shift the cost of new nuclear power plants onto utility ratepayers and taxpayers.

summary.text: Alina Bonsell is the Republican and Block Mamdani Party nominee challenging incumbent Liz Krueger. A 20-year East Side resident who says she came to the U.S. as a child when her family fled the Soviet Union as Jewish refugees, she describes a career in the pharmaceutical, biotech, healthcare and private sectors. She previously ran unsuccessfully for New York City Council District 5 in 2025 and is running on public safety, tax relief and economic growth.

background.text: According to her Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey, she came to the United States as a child when her family fled the Soviet Union as Jewish refugees; in an earlier survey response she said her family immigrated in 1989 when she was a small child.
Earned a bachelor's degree from Hofstra University.
Describes approximately 20 years of professional experience in the pharmaceutical, biotech, and healthcare private sectors (an earlier survey response gave 15 years).
Describes herself as a mother and a 20-year resident of Manhattan's East Side.
Ran for New York City Council District 5 in 2025 on the Republican line and lost to incumbent Julie Menin, 73.7% to 26.0%.
Advanced without a primary opponent in the June 2026 Republican primary for State Senate District 28 and also holds the Block Mamdani Party line.

priorities.text: Restore public safety by repealing bail reform, enforcing quality-of-life laws, and giving law enforcement more tools and support.
priorities.quote: Bail reform has failed! Repeat offenders cycle through the system while law-abiding residents pay the price. It's time to repeal these policies, restore accountability, and give law enforcement the support and tools they need to do their jobs.

priorities.text: Cut government waste and fraud and return savings as targeted tax relief, including exempting young professionals and single working parents from certain state taxes and protecting 401(k) withdrawals from state taxation up to cost-of-living thresholds.
priorities.quote: New York has a spending problem, not a revenue problem. The answer isn't to tax more, it's to govern better.

priorities.text: Promote economic growth and innovation, including lifting the fracking ban, opposing shutdowns of data centers, repealing congestion pricing, and expanding charter schools.
priorities.quote: Lift the fracking ban. Stop shutting down data centers. Repeal the congestion tax. Expand charter schools so every parent has a choice, not just those zoned for failing schools.

priorities.text: Reform family court and address neighborhood overdevelopment and shelter-placement policy.

positions.summary: Campaign platform calls for repealing bail reform, enforcing quality-of-life laws, and giving law enforcement more tools and support.
positions.quote: Public safety isn't a political issue, it's the foundation of every thriving community.

positions.summary: Campaign platform calls for repealing Manhattan's congestion pricing toll.
Campaign platform calls for expanding charter schools so parents zoned for lower-performing schools have another option.
positions.quote: Expand charter schools so every parent has a choice, not just those zoned for failing schools.

positions.summary: Platform frames New York's fiscal problems as a spending problem rather than a revenue problem and calls for tax relief rather than new taxes.
positions.quote: New York has a spending problem, not a revenue problem. The answer isn't to tax more, it's to govern better.

positions.summary: Platform calls for lifting the state's fracking ban and investing in nuclear power rather than continued expansion of solar.
positions.quote: real energy policy, lifting the fracking ban and investing in zero-emission nuclear power, not doubling down on solar that can't meet our needs

researchNotes: Krueger's positions are drawn from her official Senate bio and press releases rather than a campaign website with an explicit platform; some commonly attributed positions (e.g., on congestion pricing or immigration) could not be confirmed with a direct citable statement and were left out rather than inferred from party. Biographical detail for Alina Bonsell is limited to her Ballotpedia profile and Candidate Connection survey; no campaign website with a biography page was loaded, and her two survey submissions give different figures for years of experience.
